title: Learning-Augmented Moment Estimation on Time-Decay Models
claim: A chain of nested instances over a stream lets two of them bracket the active window, giving a good approximation.
layout: Single panel, stacked horizontal bars aligned right, dashed vertical window boundary
description: A single schematic diagram of horizontal bars along a timeline. At the bottom is a 'Stream' row: a thin line on the left, then a red-pink gradient bar from a dashed vertical line to the right end. This is labeled 'Active elements in sliding window'. Above it are four nested bars, labeled ALG^(t1) through ALG^(t4) on the right. All bars end at the same right edge but start at progressively later times. ALG^(t1) is the longest and is white. ALG^(t2) is filled with a purple-pink gradient and starts just left of the dashed line. ALG^(t3) and ALG^(t4) are short white bars that start to the right of it. The dashed line shows the window start, which falls between the starts of t2 and t3, so the t2 and t3 bars bracket the window. The eye goes first to the colored bars.
caption: Example of smooth histogram framework. Here $\ALG^{(t_2)}$ and $\ALG^{(t_3)}$ sandwich the active elements and are thus good approximations of the sliding window.
abstract: Motivated by the prevalence and success of machine learning, a line of recent work has studied learning-augmented algorithms in the streaming model. These results have shown that for natural and practical oracles implemented with machine learning models, we can obtain streaming algorithms with improved space efficiency that are otherwise provably impossible. On the other hand, our understanding is much more limited when items are weighted unequally, for example, in the sliding-window model, where older data must be expunged from the dataset, e.g., by privacy regulation laws. In this paper, we utilize an oracle for the heavy-hitters of datasets to give learning-augmented algorithms for a number of fundamental problems, such as norm/moment estimation, frequency estimation, cascaded norms, and rectangular moment estimation, in the time-decay setting. We complement our theoretical results with a number of empirical evaluations that demonstrate the practical efficiency of our algorithms on real and synthetic datasets.
